I asked about media bias detection and used the topic analysis feature. A minute or so later, I had a list of concepts with citations and links to papers I can look at further. This feels like an amazing tool to do literature overviews and to dive into new academic domains.

Elicit's own guidance: 'A good rule of thumb is to assume that around 90% of the information you see in Elicit is accurate... it's very important for you to check the work in Elicit closely.' A 90% accuracy rate seems like the sweet spot between annoying and good enough to publish for dishonest careerists.

I gave it a topic I researched in depth recently. It gave me mostly incorrect summaries (one said hypothesis X is confirmed; nope it hasn't), missed key papers, dug up obscure and irrelevant ones. Par for the course with LLMs.
It seems like it should hallucinate less, as it directly quotes, but nope, it still hallucinates just as much and then gives a quote that directly contradicts its statement.
Testing Elicit gave me quite a bit worse results than using PaperQA by futurehouse. While paperqa could understand a bit of the nuance of a scientific query, elicit did not.
The first issue I noticed was with LaTeX syntax being presented in search results, e.g. malformed math notation appearing in 'Most Relevant Sentence' on my favorites page for a paper.

I tried abstract summarization with a whitepaper for Cassandra's 'CEP-15: General Purpose Transactions', and it came up with completely made-up facts such as describing the ACCORD algorithm (not an acronym) as something invented. I would suggest tuning this feature to be a bit less creative.

I also second the earlier complaint that the follow-up email is spam. I unsubscribed and reported it as such. I never signed up for this and was never warned I would sign up or given the option not to. Do better.
The 'Positive reframe' task setting is fun: 'Don't stab me with that knife' --> 'There are lots of ways that person can hurt me other than by stabbing me with a knife'
